passage:
“Uday Chacha, look!”
Rafiq stood in the hall with every button of his shirt done up, chest pushed out, chin high.
“You did all of them yourself?”
“All by myself!” He puffed his chest even more and marched in a circle.
“Wah! Come show Dadi's friends.”
In the next room were four ladies with tea. Rafiq stopped at the door, and his chest sank. He slid behind Uday's leg and peeked out.
“Okay,” said Uday quietly. “Show them later, when you're ready.”
Rafiq nodded into his knee.

qa.q: What had Rafiq done all by himself?
qa.a: He had done up every button of his shirt.

qa.q: What changed in Rafiq's feelings when he reached the door?
qa.a: He went from proud and bold, chest out, to shy and wary in front of four strangers, which is why he hid behind Uday's leg.

qa.q: Which choice by Uday worked, and why?
qa.a: He let Rafiq show the buttons later instead of pushing him to perform, giving him time to warm up.

qa.q: What would change if Uday had pulled Rafiq into the room?
qa.a: Rafiq might feel embarrassed and upset, and his proud moment could turn into a bad one.

grounding: A preschooler stands tall with chest out after a success, then hides behind an adult's leg when shy, and is given warm-up time.

passage:
Note by Jyoti, nursery teacher, after family day.
This week Farhan finally climbed to the top of the climbing frame. He stood up there with his chest out and fists on his hips, shouting, “I'm the king!” Today, at family day, I asked him to show the parents. He walked to the frame, saw the crowd, and pressed himself behind my legs. I told him, “You can just watch today.” After the parents had moved on to the art table, he climbed it quietly and waved to his mother from the top.

qa.q: What did Farhan shout from the top of the climbing frame?
qa.a: “I'm the king!”

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when he pressed himself behind Jyoti's legs?
qa.a: He felt shy and wary with the crowd of parents watching, even though he had felt proud and bold when he climbed alone.

qa.q: What went right in how Jyoti handled the moment?
qa.a: Jyoti didn't push him to perform and let him watch, and he chose to climb once the crowd moved away.

qa.q: How might Farhan's mother feel when he waved from the top?
qa.a: She was probably proud and happy to see him do it in his own time.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a child's proud chest-out stance after a success and his shrinking with a crowd, eased by warm-up time.

passage: Raghav carried the small brass pot of water all the way from the hand pump without spilling. At the door he set it down and stood tall, chest puffed, grinning at Jyoti Dadi. “Shabash!” she said. That evening at the temple, the priest asked the children to sing. Raghav's chest caved in. He grabbed the end of Dadi's sari and hid behind her. Dadi stroked his head. “He'll sing another day,” she told the priest. On the walk home, Raghav sang loudly to the buffaloes.

qa.q: What did Raghav carry from the hand pump?
qa.a: The small brass pot of water.

qa.q: How can you tell that Raghav felt proud when he set down the pot?
qa.a: He stood tall with his chest puffed and grinned at Dadi. Later, at the temple, his caved-in chest showed he felt shy instead.

qa.q: What did Dadi do that helped Raghav?
qa.a: She stroked his head and told the priest he would sing another day, protecting him from pressure.

qa.q: How might the priest see Raghav hiding?
qa.a: The priest might see it as ordinary shyness in a small child and not mind, especially after Dadi's words.

grounding: A child stands tall after a success but shrinks behind his grandmother when asked to perform, and she gives him time.

passage: Music hour at the preschool. When Yusuf Sir played the drum song, Sonali jumped up, spun round and round, clapping over her head. She bumped a chair. Yusuf Sir could have said, “Sit properly.” Instead he put down the drum, stood up and spun too, slowly, arms wide. Sonali laughed so hard she had to stop. Then she took his hand and they spun together till the song ended. Afterwards she flopped on the mat, breathing hard, and sat still for the story.

qa.q: What song made Sonali jump up and spin?
qa.a: The drum song.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling as she spun and clapped?
qa.a: She was full of joy and delight at the music. The spinning may also have helped her let out energy, since she sat still for the story afterwards.

qa.q: Why was joining in a good choice for Yusuf Sir?
qa.a: It shared her joy and built a bond, and she settled on her own afterwards without any correcting.

qa.q: How might Yusuf Sir feel spinning beside Sonali?
qa.a: He likely feels close to her and enjoys sharing her delight, laughing along instead of worrying about the chair. 😊

grounding: A preschooler spins and claps for joy at music, and her teacher joins in rather than correcting her.

passage: I'm Vikas, from the flat above. On Sunday the first rain came, and I heard shrieks below. Kishore was out on the balcony in his vest, stamping his feet, twirling and clapping at the sky. His grandmother came out. I expected her to call him in. Instead, she tucked up her sari, held out her hands and swayed with him. They danced in a slow circle, both laughing. I don't know how long he'd waited for rain, but he looked like he'd won something.

qa.q: What was Kishore wearing on the balcony?
qa.a: His vest.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling as he twirled and clapped at the sky?
qa.a: He was joyful and excited that the first rain had come. Vikas could not be sure, but it looked like a big celebration.

qa.q: What did Kishore's grandmother do that strengthened their bond?
qa.a: She joined in and danced with him instead of calling him in, sharing his delight.

qa.q: How did the scene look to Vikas?
qa.a: It surprised and warmed Vikas, who expected a scolding and saw a shared dance instead.

grounding: A neighbour observes a child dancing for joy at the first rain, and his grandmother joins in.

passage:
Vidya's birthday, Friday: when the music started, she spun around the room. “Careful, you'll fall,” said Arnab, her father. She stopped and sat down.
Saturday: Vidya danced to the radio in the kitchen, then glanced at Arnab and stopped again.
Sunday: The radio came on. This time Arnab put down his cup, stood up and did a silly twirl. Vidya stared, then burst out laughing and clapped. They danced together, bumping hips, until Amma came in and joined them too.

qa.q: What did Arnab say when Vidya spun at her birthday?
qa.a: “Careful, you'll fall.”

qa.q: What does Vidya glancing at Arnab and stopping on Saturday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt unsure whether dancing was allowed, and a little shy after being told to be careful. Her joy was being held back.

qa.q: What changed on Sunday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Arnab joined in with a silly twirl instead of correcting, which showed her that her joy was welcome.

qa.q: How might Amma see the three of them dancing?
qa.a: She would likely feel happy and included, seeing the family share Vidya's delight.

grounding: Over three days, a father learns that joining a preschooler's dance builds bonding more than correcting her.

passage: At the park in Seoul, Jin and Zeynep raced to the slide. Zeynep touched it first. Jin stopped, turned his back and walked off to the bench, shoulders stiff. His father didn't follow him with questions. He waited a minute, then called in a calm voice, “Jin, the slide's still here when you're ready. Zeynep's waiting for a rematch.” Jin sat for a while, kicking the sand. Then he got up, walked slowly back and said, “Best of three.”

qa.q: Where did Jin walk off to?
qa.a: To the bench.

qa.q: What might Jin have been feeling as he walked off with stiff shoulders?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and embarrassed about losing the race, and wanted some space. He might also have felt a bit angry at himself.

qa.q: Why did the father's calm invitation work?
qa.a: He gave Jin space and time instead of following him with demands, and left the door open to come back.

qa.q: How might Zeynep have felt when Jin walked away?
qa.a: She might have felt confused or worried that he was angry with her, and relieved when he came back for a rematch.

grounding: A young child turns away and walks off after losing a race, and a calm invitation to return works.

passage: Sports hour at the community centre: Ujjwal grabbed the big red ball. “That one's for the older group,” said Rajni, the coach. Ujjwal dropped it, turned round and walked to the far corner, his face to the wall. Rajni didn't go after him. She set up the small balls and called out, “Ujjwal, when you're ready, there's a green ball with your name on it.” Ujjwal stayed in the corner, then peeped over his shoulder. A few minutes later he came back and picked up the green ball.

qa.q: What colour ball did Rajni offer Ujjwal?
qa.a: A green ball.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal walking off to face the wall suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt upset and embarrassed after being refused the big ball, and needed a moment alone. It could also have been anger at the rule.

qa.q: What could Rajni do next time to avoid the upset?
qa.a: She could explain before the game which balls are for which group, so the refusal doesn't come as a surprise.

qa.q: What would change if Rajni had followed him and insisted he play?
qa.a: Ujjwal might dig in and refuse, and the upset would last longer.

grounding: A young child walks off after a refusal, and his coach's calm invitation to return works better than following him.

passage: I'm Swati, Neelam's cousin. At the fair, Neelam's mother said no to a second ice cream. Neelam turned her back and walked away toward the gate, arms swinging hard. I thought she'd get lost, but her mother just kept her in sight and called, “Neelam, I'm here by the swings when you're ready.” Neelam stood at the gate for a minute, then came back and leaned against her mother's side. I couldn't tell if she was angry or sad, but she held her mother's hand after that.

qa.q: What did Neelam's mother say no to?
qa.a: A second ice cream.

qa.q: What might Neelam have been feeling when she walked away toward the gate?
qa.a: She might have been angry or sad, or both, and wanted space after the refusal. Swati could not tell which.

qa.q: Which choice by Neelam's mother worked?
qa.a: She kept Neelam in sight and gave a calm invitation to return instead of chasing her with demands.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt watching Neelam walk off?
qa.a: Swati felt worried that Neelam might get lost, and was relieved when she came back.

grounding: A cousin observes a young child walk off after a refusal, and her mother's calm invitation brings her back.

passage: When the fire alarm rang during the school drill, Zubin clapped both hands over his ears and squeezed his eyes shut. He didn't move. Lalremsiami Ma'am knelt, didn't pull his hands away, and said close to his cheek, “It's very loud. Keep your hands there. Hold my arm with your elbow.” She walked him out with the class, his hands still over his ears. Outside, she led him to the quiet side of the ground under the tree. Slowly, Zubin lowered his hands.

qa.q: Where did the teacher lead Zubin outside?
qa.a: To the quiet side of the ground under the tree.

qa.q: What does Zubin covering his ears and shutting his eyes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the loud alarm was too much and he felt frightened, so he was protecting himself. He may also have been confused about what was happening.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami Ma'am do that respected Zubin's limit?
qa.a: She let him keep his hands over his ears, walked him out safely, and took him somewhere quieter.

qa.q: What would change if the teacher had pulled his hands away?
qa.a: Zubin would likely feel more frightened and learn that his way of coping wasn't allowed.

grounding: A preschooler covers his ears and eyes at a loud alarm, and his teacher respects it and offers a quieter space.

passage: I'm Disha, the neighbour. At the Ganesh procession, the drums were thundering past our gate. Sarika, who is four, pressed both hands over her ears and hid her face in her father's leg. He didn't say, “Don't be scared.” He picked her up and walked into the side lane where it was quieter. From there she could still see the lights. After a while she took one hand off her ear, and then the other, and watched the idol go by, eyes wide.

qa.q: Where did Sarika's father take her?
qa.a: Into the side lane where it was quieter.

qa.q: What might Sarika have been feeling when she pressed her hands over her ears?
qa.a: She was probably overwhelmed and frightened by the loud drums. Later, with wide eyes, she seemed to be feeling awe at the procession.

qa.q: What did Sarika's father do well?
qa.a: He respected her signal and took her somewhere quieter where she could still enjoy the lights at her own pace.

qa.q: How does Disha see the father's choice?
qa.a: Disha seems to notice and approve that he didn't dismiss her fear but found a way for her to still take part.

grounding: A neighbour observes a preschooler covering her ears at loud drums and her father offering a quieter space.

passage:
Monday: The pressure cooker whistled. Jahnavi screamed and covered her ears. Sahil, her father, said, “It's just a whistle, don't be silly.” She cried harder.
Wednesday: Sahil said, “The cooker is going to whistle soon. Do you want to go to the balcony?” Jahnavi went, hands ready near her ears.
Friday: Jahnavi saw the cooker on the stove, put her hands over her ears and announced, “Whistle time, I'm going to the balcony.” Sahil smiled. “Good plan.”

qa.q: Where did Jahnavi go before the whistle?
qa.a: To the balcony.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling on Monday when she cried harder?
qa.a: She was scared of the loud whistle, and felt more upset when her fear was called silly.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Wednesday that helped?
qa.a: Sahil gave a warning and offered a quieter place, respecting her need to cover her ears.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel on Friday when Jahnavi makes her own plan?
qa.a: He likely feels proud and relieved that she has learned to protect herself calmly.

grounding: Over a week, a preschooler learns that covering her ears and moving away from a loud noise is allowed, after her father respects it.

passage: The wedding hall was packed, and Farida had five minutes to get Aadhya changed for the photos. On the way, a distant aunty grabbed Aadhya and squeezed her into a hug, kissing her cheek. Aadhya stiffened, ducked, and pushed at the aunty's arm. The aunty laughed and pulled her closer. Farida stepped in. “She doesn't want a hug right now. High five, Aadhya?” Aadhya gave a tiny high five. Walking away, Farida said, “You're allowed to say no. If anyone keeps doing it, tell me.”

qa.q: What did Farida offer instead of the hug?
qa.a: A high five.

qa.q: What did Aadhya's stiffening and ducking show about how she felt?
qa.a: They showed she was uncomfortable and did not want the hug. The aunty seemed to read it as shyness, but Aadhya was signalling no.

qa.q: How did Farida protect Aadhya, even in a rush?
qa.a: She stepped in straight away, spoke up for Aadhya, offered a high five instead, and told her she could say no and tell her if it happened again.

qa.q: How might the aunty see Farida's words?
qa.a: She might feel a little embarrassed or surprised, but she also learns that Aadhya's no should be respected.

grounding: A child stiffens and pulls away from an unwanted hug, and her mother respects the signal and teaches her she can say no and tell.

passage: At the colony gate, Anand Uncle from the next building bent down, ruffled Baljeet's hair and held out his arms. “Come, give Uncle a big hug!” Baljeet stepped back behind his mother, his body stiff. His mother said calmly, “He doesn't want to, and that's okay.” Anand Uncle straightened up and nodded. “Fair enough. High five, then?” Baljeet thought, then slapped his palm. At home, his mother said, “You can say, ‘No, thank you.’ And if someone doesn't stop, come and tell me.” Baljeet practised it on his teddy.

qa.q: What did Baljeet practise on his teddy?
qa.a: Saying, “No, thank you.”

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when he stepped behind his mother?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable and did not want the hug, and his stiff body showed it. He may also have felt shy with Uncle.

qa.q: What did Baljeet's mother teach him at home?
qa.a: She gave him the words “No, thank you” and told him to come and tell her if someone doesn't stop.

qa.q: How did Anand Uncle respond, and what does it show?
qa.a: He accepted the no and offered a high five, which shows a caring adult respecting a child's signal.

grounding: A child pulls back from a neighbour's hug, the adults respect it, and he practises saying no and telling a trusted adult.

passage:
“Papa, can I not go to tuition tomorrow?”
Harish put down his phone. “What's happened, Ojas?”
“A big boy squeezes me in a hug. Really tight. I say stop and he doesn't.”
“How does it feel?”
“Scary. I can't breathe.”
Harish knelt beside him. “Thank you for telling me. It's not your fault, and you were right to say stop. Your body is yours.”
“Will you tell Miss?”
“Right now.” He called the tuition teacher while Ojas held his hand, and she promised to keep the boy away from Ojas and to speak to his parents that evening.

qa.q: What did Ojas say he does when the big boy hugs him?
qa.a: He says stop, and the boy doesn't stop.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling about the tight hugs?
qa.a: He felt scared and trapped, saying he couldn't breathe, and worried enough to want to skip tuition.

qa.q: What did Harish do that a caring adult should do?
qa.a: He listened, thanked Ojas, said it was not his fault and that he was right to say stop, and called the tuition teacher straight away while Ojas held his hand.

qa.q: How might the tuition teacher see Harish's call?
qa.a: The teacher would likely take it seriously and act, keeping the boy away from Ojas and speaking to his parents that evening.

grounding: A child's pulling away from tight hugs is a valid no; when the pressure continues he tells his father, who acts the same day.

subtype: Covering the mouth when shy or surprised [Expressing]
passage: I'm Manoj, Sabina's big brother. On Sunday the neighbours came for tea, and Mummy served the cake. Sabina, who's five, announced, “Mummy said the cake got burnt at the bottom!” Then her eyes went huge and she clapped both hands over her mouth. Everyone went quiet for a second. I couldn't tell if she was embarrassed or trying not to laugh; her shoulders were shaking. Mummy smiled at her, and the neighbour aunty laughed. “Burnt is my favourite part,” she said. Sabina peeped out from behind her fingers.

qa.q: What did Sabina announce about the cake?
qa.a: That Mummy said the cake got burnt at the bottom.

qa.q: What might Sabina's hands over her mouth show about how she felt?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed at letting slip something private, or she may have been giggling at her own mischief; Manoj couldn't tell which.

qa.q: What helped Sabina feel safe after the slip?
qa.a: Mummy's gentle smile and the neighbour aunty's joke about liking burnt cake showed her she wasn't in trouble.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when Sabina said the cake was burnt?
qa.a: She might have felt a moment of embarrassment, but her smile shows she chose to take it lightly.

grounding: A brother observes his sister cover her mouth after a slip, where it could mean embarrassment or mischief, and a smile reassures her.

subtype: Covering the mouth when shy or surprised [Expressing]
passage:
Monday: A rainbow appeared over the colony. Ankita put both hands over her mouth and stared, silent. Kavitha, her mother, knelt beside her. “Beautiful, na?”
Wednesday: At the park, Ankita told her friend, “Your mummy's making you a surprise cake!” Then she slapped a hand over her mouth, cheeks pink. Kavitha smiled gently. “Oops. It's okay.”
Friday: Kavitha wore a funny hat to the market. Ankita covered her mouth, eyes sparkling, and giggled behind her hand the whole way home.

qa.q: What did Ankita tell her friend on Wednesday?
qa.a: “Your mummy's making you a surprise cake!”

qa.q: What does Ankita's pink cheeks with her hand over her mouth on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt embarrassed about giving away the surprise. On Monday the same gesture showed awe, and on Friday it hid amusement.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha's gentle smile help on Wednesday?
qa.a: It showed Ankita the slip wasn't a disaster, so she could feel safe instead of ashamed.

qa.q: How might Ankita's friend feel about the spoiled surprise?
qa.a: She would probably feel excited to hear about the cake, not upset, even though it was meant to be a secret.

grounding: Over a week, one child covers her mouth in awe, embarrassment and giggles, and context shows which each time.

subtype: Covering the mouth when shy or surprised [Expressing]
passage: The power went out just as the birthday candles were lit, so the room glowed only with their light. Tushar's uncle opened a basket in the dark, and a tiny white puppy poked its head out. Tushar gasped and pressed both hands over his mouth. He didn't move. His eyes were wet and shining in the candlelight. Vikas, his father, couldn't tell if he was scared or amazed. He knelt and smiled. “It's okay. He's yours to hold, if you want.” Tushar's hands came down. “Mine?”

qa.q: What was in the basket?
qa.a: A tiny white puppy.

qa.q: What might Tushar have been feeling with his hands over his mouth and wet eyes?
qa.a: He was most likely amazed and overjoyed, in shy surprise. In the dark, Vikas couldn't be sure if he was a little scared too.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that helped?
qa.a: He knelt and smiled and told Tushar he could hold the puppy if he wanted, which helped him feel safe to respond.

qa.q: What would change if the lights had been on?
qa.a: Vikas could have read Tushar's face more easily and known sooner whether it was joy or fear.

grounding: A child covers his mouth in shy surprise at a gift, and a gentle smile helps him feel safe.

passage:
Note by Vaibhav, swimming coach, Saturday.
Before his first jump from the side, Sumit stood chewing his thumbnail and picking at the string of his shorts. He wasn't being naughty; he was waiting and nervous. I didn't tell him to stop. I gave him the squeezy ring we keep for the little ones and said, “Squeeze, and blow out like bubbles, three times.” He did, then jumped in. I've asked his mother to try the same breathing at home before bedtime story.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav give Sumit?
qa.a: The squeezy ring kept for the little ones.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling as he chewed his thumbnail?
qa.a: He was nervous about his first jump from the side, and the chewing was a way to soothe himself while he waited.

qa.q: What could Sumit's mother try at home, and why?
qa.a: She could practise the same breathing with him before the bedtime story, so he has a calm habit ready when he feels nervous.

qa.q: What would change if Vaibhav had punished the nail-chewing?
qa.a: Sumit would likely feel more anxious and ashamed, and might not have jumped at all.

grounding: The coach's note shows a preschooler chewing a nail and fidgeting while nervous, and a fidget toy and deep breaths helping instead of punishment.

passage: At the bus stand, Eshaan waited with his mother, Arohi, for his father's bus from the city. It was late. Eshaan chewed the corner of his nail, then picked at a loose thread on his shirt till it made a hole. Arohi saw it but didn't scold. She found a smooth, cool pebble near the tea stall and put it in his hand. “Rub this. And let's breathe like a balloon.” They breathed in and out. When the bus horn sounded, Eshaan dropped the pebble and ran.

qa.q: What did Arohi put in Eshaan's hand?
qa.a: A smooth, cool pebble.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling while he waited for the late bus?
qa.a: He was probably anxious and impatient about his father's bus being late, and picking the thread soothed him.

qa.q: Why did giving the pebble work better than scolding?
qa.a: It gave his hands something calming to do and treated the picking as worry, not naughtiness.

qa.q: How might Arohi have been feeling while they waited?
qa.a: She may have been a bit anxious too about the late bus, but she stayed calm to help Eshaan.

grounding: A preschooler chews a nail and picks at clothes while waiting nervously, and his mother offers a soothing object and breathing.

passage: The dentist's waiting room in Vancouver smelled of mint. Tuan sat on his mother's lap, chewing the collar of his T-shirt until it was soaked. Then he bit his nails. His mother gently moved his hand. At the desk, Hiroshi, the receptionist, noticed and came over with a squishy toy shaped like a tooth. “Lots of kids squeeze this while they wait.” Tuan squeezed it hard. Hiroshi showed him how to breathe in through the nose, out through the mouth. Tuan copied, chewing nothing.

qa.q: What shape was the squishy toy?
qa.a: A tooth.

qa.q: What does Tuan chewing his collar suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he was nervous about seeing the dentist and was soothing himself. It could also just be a habit when waiting.

qa.q: Which choice by Hiroshi helped, and why?
qa.a: Offering a squishy toy and breathing gave Tuan a calmer way to soothe his nerves without being told off.

qa.q: How might Tuan's mother feel when Hiroshi comes over?
qa.a: She is probably relieved and grateful for help keeping Tuan calm.

grounding: A preschooler fidgets and chews his collar and nails while nervously waiting, and a fidget toy and breathing help.

passage: The train would leave in five minutes. Deepak Mama bent down on the crowded platform. “Raghav, give Mama a kiss goodbye!” Raghav leaned back and shook his head. People jostled past with bags. His mother said, “Raghav can choose. Hug, wave or high five?” Raghav held up his palm. Deepak Mama slapped it, grinning. “Best high five in Pune!” He climbed aboard and waved from the door. Raghav waved back with both hands until the train was gone.

qa.q: What did Raghav choose instead of a kiss?
qa.a: A high five.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when he leaned back and shook his head?
qa.a: He didn't want to kiss and felt uncomfortable being asked, possibly also rushed and crowded on the busy platform.

qa.q: What did Raghav's mother do that taught him his body belongs to him?
qa.a: She gave him a choice of hug, wave or high five, even with a relative and little time.

qa.q: How did Deepak Mama respond, and what does it show?
qa.a: He accepted the high five happily, showing that love can be shared in ways the child chooses.

grounding: On a crowded platform, a preschooler chooses a high five instead of a kiss, and his uncle accepts it.

passage: Pranav ran to his friend Isha in the housing society park with his arms out, then stopped. His mother Kavitha had been teaching him to ask first. “Isha, can I hug you?” Isha shook her head. “No, I'm sweaty.” Pranav's arms dropped. He looked at Kavitha. She nodded. “You asked, and she said no. What else can you do?” Pranav thought. “Wave?” He waved. Isha waved back and grabbed his hand. “Come, let's go to the seesaw!”

qa.q: Why did Isha say no to a hug?
qa.a: Because she was sweaty.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when his arms dropped?
qa.a: He felt a bit disappointed and unsure what to do after Isha said no. Looking at Kavitha shows he wanted help.

qa.q: How did Kavitha help Pranav handle the no?
qa.a: She named what happened and asked what else he could do, so he found the wave himself.

qa.q: How might Isha see Pranav asking first?
qa.a: She likely feels respected and comfortable, since she could say no and still play with him.

grounding: A preschooler learns to ask before hugging and to accept a no, choosing a wave instead.

passage:
“Vasudha! Come here, give Bhavna Maasi a big kiss!”
Vasudha stayed by the door, holding the handle.
Maasi paused. “Hmm. Do you want a hug, a wave, or a high five?”
Vasudha thought. “…Wave.”
“A wave it is.” Maasi waved with both hands.
Vasudha waved back, smiling.
Later, her mother said, “Your Maasi loves you even with a wave, right?”
“Right,” said Vasudha. “Maybe tomorrow a hug.”
“Only if you want,” said Maasi.

qa.q: What did Vasudha choose?
qa.a: A wave.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling as she stayed by the door holding the handle?
qa.a: She was probably shy or unsure and did not want a kiss yet. Later she felt comfortable enough to smile and wave.

qa.q: How did Bhavna Maasi respond when Vasudha didn't come?
qa.a: She paused and offered a choice of hug, wave or high five, and happily accepted the wave.

qa.q: How might Vasudha's mother see Maasi's choice?
qa.a: She would likely be glad, because it teaches Vasudha that her body belongs to her even with relatives.

grounding: A preschooler chooses a wave instead of a kiss with her aunt, and the aunt accepts it.

passage:
Monday: Vishal, Ojas's father, read him a picture book about touch. “Safe touch feels good, like a high five or a hug you want. Private parts are the ones your underwear covers. Nobody should touch them or ask you to keep touch a secret.”
Wednesday: At the clinic, the doctor asked, “Can I check your tummy?” with Papa right there. Ojas said, “Papa's here, so okay.”
Friday: Ojas told Papa, “Cousin tickled me too much and I said stop.” Papa hugged him. “Good job saying stop.” That evening he told the cousin tickling stops when someone says stop.

qa.q: What did the doctor ask Ojas on Wednesday?
qa.a: “Can I check your tummy?”

qa.q: What does Ojas's comment at the clinic show about his thinking?
qa.a: It shows he felt safe and trusted the check because Papa was there and the doctor asked first. He was using what he learned from the book.

qa.q: What did Vishal do on Friday, and why was it right?
qa.a: He praised Ojas for saying stop and spoke to the cousin that evening, showing Ojas that his no matters and adults will act.

qa.q: How might the cousin see the tickling rule?
qa.a: The cousin might have thought tickling was just fun, but learns that it stops when someone says stop.

grounding: Over a week, a child learns about safe touch and private parts, and his father acts when he reports tickling that felt too much.

passage: School was starting in ten minutes and Nitin was hunting for Disha's shoe when she said, “Papa, a big boy in the van said let's play a secret game. He tried to put his hand under my shorts. I pushed him and moved seats.” Nitin stopped. He sat on the floor beside her. “Thank you for telling me. You did exactly right. It is not your fault.” He listened to all of it. Then he rang the school principal, drove Disha himself, and stayed while the principal took notes.

qa.q: What did Disha do when the boy tried to touch her?
qa.a: She pushed him and moved seats.

qa.q: What might Disha have been feeling when she told her father?
qa.a: She was probably confused and scared by what the boy did, and worried about the secret game. Telling Papa shows she trusted him.

qa.q: What did Nitin do that a trusted adult should do?
qa.a: He stopped everything, listened calmly, said it was not her fault, and told the principal the same morning while staying with her.

qa.q: How might the principal see Nitin's report?
qa.a: The principal would take it seriously and act to keep Disha and other children safe in the van.

grounding: A child tells her father about unsafe touch and a request for secrecy, and he responds the same morning by listening and telling the school.

passage: In the city nursery, Keerthana Ma'am held up two cards: a hand giving a high five, and a stop sign. “Safe touch feels okay, like a hug from Amma when you want one. Unsafe touch feels muddled or scary inside, or someone touches where your swimsuit covers.” Hafsa's hand went up. “What about secrets?” “Surprises are fine, like a birthday present, because everyone finds out soon. But secrets about touch? Never. Tell a grown-up you trust.” Hafsa nodded seriously. “I'll tell Ammi and you.”

qa.q: What did Keerthana Ma'am hold up?
qa.a: Two cards: a hand giving a high five, and a stop sign.

qa.q: What was Hafsa thinking about when she asked about secrets?
qa.a: She was curious and a little unsure how secrets fit with the touch rules, and wanted to understand the difference.

qa.q: How did Keerthana Ma'am explain surprises versus secrets?
qa.a: She said surprises are fine because everyone finds out soon, but secrets about touch should never be kept and should be told to a trusted grown-up.

qa.q: How might Hafsa's Ammi feel hearing that Hafsa would tell her?
qa.a: She would likely feel reassured and trusted, knowing Hafsa sees her as a safe person to tell.

grounding: A teacher helps preschoolers learn safe and unsafe touch and that secrets about touch should be told to a trusted adult.

passage: At the dairy counter in the village, Uday stood so close to Baljeet Singh that his nose nearly touched the counter's edge by the man's elbow. Baljeet laughed and stepped back. “Arre, too close, little one!” He stretched out his arm. “See? This much space for talking. With your amma you can stand close, but with shopkeepers, one arm.” Uday stretched his arm out too and stepped back till his fingers touched the counter. “Like this?” “Perfect. Now, how much milk?”

qa.q: What did Baljeet Singh stretch out to show the space?
qa.a: His arm.

qa.q: What might Uday have been thinking when he stood so close?
qa.a: He was probably curious and excited, not aware that standing so close could make someone uncomfortable. He wanted to be part of the talk.

qa.q: What made Baljeet's coaching work?
qa.a: He used a clear, friendly demonstration with his arm and simple words, and explained that family can be closer.

qa.q: How might Uday's amma see this lesson?
qa.a: She might be pleased that he learned arm's length kindly, and that he knows he can still be close to her.

grounding: A child crowds a shopkeeper and learns kindly that an arm's length is a fair distance, while family may stand closer.

passage: At circle time in the kindergarten in Madrid, the children crowded around Elif to see her new shoes. She froze, arms tight at her sides, and her lip wobbled. Valentina, the teacher, noticed. “Everyone, let's make our circle bigger. Stretch your arms out and take one step back.” The children did. Then Valentina crouched by Elif. “When it's too crowded, you can say, ‘Space, please.’” Elif nodded. She tried it the next time a friend leaned in, and the friend stepped back.

qa.q: What did the children crowd around Elif to see?
qa.a: Her new shoes.

qa.q: What did Elif's freezing and wobbling lip suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and uncomfortable with so many children close. She might also have felt shy about being the centre of attention.

qa.q: What small step did Valentina give Elif?
qa.a: She gave her the words “Space, please” to use when it is too crowded.

qa.q: How might the other children see Elif's freezing?
qa.a: They were excited about the shoes and probably didn't notice she was uncomfortable until the teacher spoke.

grounding: A child freezes when crowded, and her teacher coaches the group about arm's length and gives her clear words.

passage: Trisha loved talking to Devika, the art helper at the community centre. But she stood right up against Devika's knees, face tipped up, talking into her chin. Devika gently held Trisha's shoulders and moved her back a little. “I love hearing about your painting. Let's talk with this much space.” She held out her arm. Trisha stepped back. “Why?” “Some people feel squished when someone is very close. With your mum you can sit on her lap.” Trisha grinned. “With you, one arm.”

qa.q: Who was Devika at the community centre?
qa.a: The art helper.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as she stood right up close?
qa.a: She was excited and fond of Devika, eager to share her painting, and didn't realise the closeness might feel squished.

qa.q: What would you advise an adult coaching a child about personal space?
qa.a: Stay warm, show the distance with an arm, and explain simply that family can be closer, as Devika did.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt with Trisha right against her knees?
qa.a: She probably felt a bit squished but also liked Trisha's affection, so she moved her back gently.

grounding: A child crowds a helper while talking and is coached gently about arm's length and closer distance with family.
